secs: Where vets can help

Every enquiry is different, but these are typical starting points for clients who contact vets:

  • A pet that has eaten something toxic or unusual.
  • Dental problems such as bad breath, broken teeth or difficulty eating.
  • An injury after a fall, fight or road accident.
  • Neutering, minor surgery or a second opinion before major surgery.
  • An older pet with stiffness, weight loss or changes in appetite.

If your situation is not listed, that is fine. Describe it in your own words and we will work out which kind of vet fits best.

What a 24-hour vet is likely to cost (POA)

Veterinary fees vary a great deal between practices, regions and ownership groups, and the CMA has looked closely at transparency in this market. A good practice will explain the consultation charge, any likely tests and the range of treatment options before you commit. Because every case is different, iComply does not publish prices: quotes come from the practice and are POA.

Ask for an itemised estimate for anything beyond a routine consultation, and ask whether written prescriptions are available if you would prefer to buy medication elsewhere. Insurers often require you to pay first and claim later, so check your policy's excess and limits.
Checking vets are qualified and regulated

Every vet practising in the UK must be registered with the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons (RCVS), and you can search the RCVS register by name before you book. Veterinary nurses have their own RCVS register too. Many practices also join the voluntary RCVS Practice Standards Scheme, which inspects premises, equipment and clinical processes.

Some vets hold further qualifications such as an RCVS certificate, advanced practitioner status or specialist status in a particular species or discipline. If your animal has a complex or unusual condition, it is reasonable to ask whether the vet treating it holds one of these, or whether they refer to someone who does.

  • Vague answers about who covers emergencies at night and at weekends
  • Pressure to agree to expensive treatment without a clear explanation of alternatives
  • Refusal to provide a written estimate or prescription when asked

Once you are introduced, these questions help you decide whether the vet is right for you:

Searching for best financial adviser near me? You probably want someone suitable, available and within reach. Financial advisers recommend how to save, invest, protect and plan for retirement based on your goals and circumstances.

We act as the middleman between you and the professional. Share a short brief and we match you with a financial adviser who has the right experience and capacity. Enquiring is free, and you are under no obligation to accept a quote.
secs: What financial advisers commonly help with

Every enquiry is different, but these are typical starting points for clients who contact financial advisers:

  • Planning for inheritance tax.
  • Reviewing scattered pensions and investments.
  • Protecting family income with life or income protection cover.
  • Investing a lump sum from savings, inheritance or a business sale.
  • Advice for business owners on extracting profits.

If your situation is not listed, that is fine. Describe it in your own words and we will work out which kind of financial adviser fits best.
Before you choose a financial adviser

These practical points are worth knowing before you speak to anyone about a financial adviser:

  • Check FCA authorisation.
  • Know whether advice is independent or restricted.
  • Agree ongoing service in writing.

A good financial adviser will talk you through each of these in plain English.
Getting ready for your first conversation

You do not need all of this to enquire, but the more you can share, the better the match:

  • Debts and other commitments
  • Any deadlines, such as a pension decision
  • Income, outgoings and savings
  • Your attitude to risk and investment experience
  • Property and mortgage details
  • Family situation and dependants

Please do not send confidential records or full files in your first message. The practice will ask for what it needs securely once you are introduced.
Looking for a financial adviser close to home

When you search for a financial adviser near you, you usually want someone reachable, available and trustworthy. Tell us your town or postcode and we look for suitable practices nearby with capacity to help.

Near-me searches return lots of results, from directories to adverts. Our role is simpler: understand your brief and introduce a suitable professional, so you do not have to work through the list alone.
Typical timescales
A first meeting is often available within a week or two. A full recommendation usually follows after the adviser has gathered information and researched options, which can take a few weeks.
What to ask before you instruct anyone

Once you are introduced, these questions help you decide whether the financial adviser is right for you:

  • Which platforms or providers do you typically use, and why?
  • What qualifications do you hold?
  • What will the ongoing service include each year?
  • How will you report on performance?
  • What happens if I want to stop ongoing advice?
  • How do you charge for initial advice and ongoing service?
Your relationship with the practice

Once introduced, the firm will explain its services and charges, then complete a fact-find with you. Advice and responsibility sit with the authorised firm. iComply does not give financial advice. The value of investments can fall as well as rise.
Qualifications and registration to look for

Financial advice in the UK is regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). Check that any adviser or firm is authorised, or is an appointed representative of an authorised firm, on the FCA register. If something goes wrong you can complain to the firm, then to the Financial Ombudsman Service, and the Financial Services Compensation Scheme may protect you if an authorised firm fails.

Advisers must tell you whether their advice is independent (considering the whole market) or restricted (limited to certain products or providers), and how they charge. Chartered status from the Chartered Insurance Institute or the Personal Finance Society, and certifications such as CFP, show advanced qualifications.

Adviser and advisor are simply two spellings of the same word. What matters is whether the person giving advice is qualified and, where the law requires it, regulated for that type of advice.

Please note that iComply is a matching service only. We are not regulated as a financial adviser, and we do not give professional advice. The practice you are introduced to is responsible for its own registration and for the work it does.
Warning signs to watch for

Most professionals are honest and competent, but it is worth knowing the warning signs:

  • Unclear or hidden charges
  • Not on the FCA register, or a clone firm using a real firm's name
  • Pressure to transfer pensions or invest quickly
  • Guaranteed high returns
How iComply matches you

1. Tell us what you need. Use the contact form, WhatsApp or phone. A few lines is enough.
  2. We review your brief. We check the type of financial adviser you need, your location and your timing.
  3. We match you. We introduce a suitable practice with capacity, usually within a few working days.
  4. You get a quote. The practice quotes you directly, POA. You decide whether to go ahead.

There is no charge to you for the introduction, and no obligation to accept any quote.
What "best" really means when choosing a financial adviser

There is no single best financial adviser for everyone. The right choice depends on your situation, how complex it is, where you are and how you like to communicate. A practice that is outstanding for one client can be a poor fit for another.

Useful signs of quality include verified registration with the right body, relevant experience with situations like yours, clear written terms, honest answers about risks, and good communication from the very first contact. Online reviews can help, but read them for patterns rather than single comments, and remember that the most visible firm is not always the most suitable.

When we match you, we look at fit rather than marketing claims: specialism, location, capacity and whether the practice can start when you need it.

  • Planning for inheritance tax and passing on assets.

Qualifications and registration to look for

Writing a will is not a reserved legal activity in England and Wales, so some will writers are not regulated. Solicitors (SRA) and chartered legal executives (CILEx) are regulated, insured and covered by the Legal Ombudsman. Looking for company commercial solicitor near me usually starts with a practical problem that needs a qualified person. Company commercial solicitors combine corporate work, such as share sales and investments, with day-to-day commercial contracts.

We act as the middleman between you and the professional. Share a short brief and we match you with a company and commercial solicitor who has the right experience and capacity. Enquiring is free, and you are under no obligation to accept a quote.
secs: Where solicitors can help

Solicitors help clients in many situations. Some of the most common are:

  • An injury or a medical treatment that went wrong.
  • A will, a lasting power of attorney or a family member's estate.
  • A dispute with an employer, landlord, business or neighbour.
  • A business contract, shareholder agreement or company sale.
  • A debt that is owed to you, or one you are being chased for.

If your situation is not listed, that is fine. Describe it in your own words and we will work out which kind of solicitor fits best.
Getting ready for your first conversation

A short, clear brief saves time on both sides. Useful details include:

  • A short timeline of what has happened, with dates
  • Any deadlines you have been given, especially court dates
  • Copies of key documents such as contracts, letters or court papers
  • How you prefer to be contacted
  • What outcome you would like
  • Whether you may be eligible for legal aid

Please do not send confidential records or full files in your first message. The practice will ask for what it needs securely once you are introduced.
Warning signs to watch for

Be cautious if you notice any of the following:

  • Guarantees about the outcome of a dispute
  • Pressure to sign immediately without time to read terms
  • Requests to send money to an account that changes by email
  • No clear costs information or client care letter
What happens after you are introduced

After the introduction, the firm will carry out identity checks and conflict checks and send a client care letter setting out who is acting for you, what they will do and how they charge. Your legal relationship is with the firm. iComply does not give legal advice and does not take part in your case.
How long things usually take

Many firms can arrange an initial conversation within a few days. Court deadlines, police interviews and limitation periods are time-critical, so include them in your enquiry. If you have a court hearing in the next few days, contact a solicitor directly as well as enquiring with us.
How our free matching service works

1. Tell us what you need. Use the contact form, WhatsApp or phone. A few lines is enough.
  2. We review your brief. We check the type of solicitor you need, your location and your timing.
  3. We match you. We introduce a suitable practice with capacity, usually within a few working days.
  4. You get a quote. The practice quotes you directly, POA. You decide whether to go ahead.

There is no charge to you for the introduction, and no obligation to accept any quote.
Before you choose a company and commercial solicitor

These practical points are worth knowing before you speak to anyone about a company and commercial solicitor:

  • Due diligence protects buyers.
  • Investment rounds need careful documentation.
  • Ask about warranties and indemnities.

A good solicitor will talk you through each of these in plain English.
What to ask before you instruct anyone

Once you are introduced, these questions help you decide whether the solicitor is right for you:

  • How much experience do you have with cases like mine?
  • How will you keep me updated?
  • What are the likely next steps and timescales?
  • What is your realistic view of my options at this stage?
  • What is your complaints procedure?
  • Who will handle my matter day to day, and who supervises them?
What a company and commercial solicitor is likely to cost (POA)

Legal fees depend on the type of matter, its complexity and who does the work. Firms commonly charge hourly rates, fixed fees for defined stages, or (in some claims) conditional fee arrangements. Regulated firms in England and Wales must publish pricing information for certain services and give you clear costs information at the outset. iComply does not publish fees; the firm will give you a POA quote.

Ask for a written estimate and for an explanation of what is not included, such as court fees, barristers' fees or experts. Ask too whether legal expenses insurance or legal aid might cover some or all of the cost.
Near me: how local matching works

When you search for a company and commercial solicitor near you, you usually want someone reachable, available and trustworthy. Tell us your town or postcode and we look for suitable practices nearby with capacity to help.

Near-me searches return lots of results, from directories to adverts. Our role is simpler: understand your brief and introduce a suitable professional, so you do not have to work through the list alone.
Qualifications and registration to look for

Solicitors in England and Wales are regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA), and you can check an individual or firm on the SRA's register. In Scotland solicitors are regulated by the Law Society of Scotland, and in Northern Ireland by the Law Society of Northern Ireland. Regulated firms must hold professional indemnity insurance and have a complaints procedure; if that does not resolve things, the Legal Ombudsman can look at service complaints in England and Wales.

The word "lawyer" is not protected on its own, so check that whoever handles your matter is a solicitor, a chartered legal executive (CILEx) or another authorised professional. Reserved activities such as conducting court litigation and certain probate and conveyancing work can only be carried out by authorised people.

iComply is not a regulator and does not provide the professional service itself. We introduce you to professionals who hold their own registrations, and we encourage you to check them on the public register.

"Lawyer" is a general word that covers solicitors, barristers, chartered legal executives and others. A solicitor is a specific regulated professional who can advise you, run your case and instruct a barrister if needed.
Can I get legal aid?

Legal aid is still available for some criminal, family (especially where there is domestic abuse), housing and immigration matters, subject to means and merits tests. A matched firm can tell you whether you are likely to qualify.

Rather than calling round, you can send one enquiry to iComply. We look at your needs, location and timing, then introduce you to a suitable tax practice. They quote you directly, POA, and you decide whether to go ahead.
secs: Common reasons people contact tax advisers

Tax advisers help clients in many situations. Some of the most common are:

  • Selling a property, shares or a business and wanting to understand the tax.
  • A VAT question that could affect pricing or cash flow.
  • A business considering investment schemes such as EIS or SEIS.
  • A contractor unsure how IR35 applies to their work.
  • Planning for inheritance tax across the family.

If your situation is not listed, that is fine. Describe it in your own words and we will work out which kind of tax adviser fits best.
What a corporation tax adviser is likely to cost (POA)

Tax advice is usually charged by time or as a fixed fee for a defined piece of work, such as a written report or handling an HMRC enquiry. Complexity, deadlines and the amount at stake all affect the quote. iComply does not publish fees; the adviser you are matched with will quote you, POA.

Ask whether the first conversation is free or chargeable, and ask for a written scope before detailed advice begins. If an HMRC enquiry is involved, ask whether you have fee protection insurance through an existing accountant.
How to check you are in safe hands

"Tax adviser" is not a protected title in the UK. The Chartered Institute of Taxation (CTA qualification) and the Association of Taxation Technicians (ATT) are the main specialist bodies, and many accountants and solicitors also advise on tax. Members of these bodies follow Professional Conduct in Relation to Taxation, a shared code covering honesty, confidentiality and dealing with HMRC.

Tax advisers who provide services for a fee must be supervised for anti-money-laundering purposes. HMRC has also been tightening standards for paid tax agents, so it is reasonable to ask about qualifications, supervision and professional indemnity insurance before you go ahead.

Adviser and advisor are simply two spellings of the same word. What matters is whether the person giving advice is qualified and, where the law requires it, regulated for that type of advice.

iComply is not a regulator and does not provide the professional service itself. We introduce you to professionals who hold their own registrations, and we encourage you to check them on the public register.

  • Any deadlines given by HMRC or a buyer or seller

  • Copies of any HMRC letters, with reference numbers

  • Relevant figures, even if they are estimates

Please do not send confidential records or full files in your first message. The practice will ask for what it needs securely once you are introduced.

Straightforward questions can often be answered within a couple of weeks. HMRC enquiries and appeals have their own deadlines, which should be included in your enquiry so we can prioritise advisers with capacity. Large transactions benefit from advice before contracts are signed, not after.
Warning signs to watch for

Be cautious if you notice any of the following:

  • Advice that relies on keeping information from HMRC
  • Pressure to act quickly without written advice
  • No professional body membership or AML supervision
  • Fees linked to a percentage of tax "saved" without clear terms
Your relationship with the practice

Once introduced, the adviser will carry out identity checks, agree a written engagement and, where needed, get your authority to speak to HMRC. Advice and responsibility for it sit with the adviser, not with iComply.

Asking a few direct questions early tells you a lot about how a practice works:

  • Will I get advice in writing that I can rely on?
  • How long will this take, and what happens next?
  • Are you CTA or ATT qualified, or a member of another body?
  • What are the main risks or uncertainties in my position?
  • Will you deal with HMRC directly on my behalf?
  • Have you dealt with situations like mine before?

These practical points are worth knowing before you speak to anyone about a corporation tax adviser:

  • R&D claims face HMRC scrutiny; get them right.
  • Group relief can shelter profits.

Using reliefs and allowances as Parliament intended is normal and legal. Aggressive avoidance schemes are a different matter and can carry serious risks. A qualified adviser will explain the difference clearly.

Good questions for your first call

Once you are introduced, these questions help you decide whether the solicitor is right for you:

  • How much experience do you have with cases like mine?
  • Who will handle my matter day to day, and who supervises them?
  • How will you keep me updated?
  • What could make costs rise, and how will you warn me?
  • How will you charge: hourly, fixed fee, or another arrangement?
  • What is your complaints procedure?
Warning signs to watch for

  • No clear costs information or client care letter

What to prepare before you enquire

A short, clear brief saves time on both sides. Useful details include:

Please do not send confidential records or full files in your first message. The practice will ask for what it needs securely once you are introduced.
How fees usually work (POA)

Legal fees depend on the type of matter, its complexity and who does the work. Firms commonly charge hourly rates, fixed fees for defined stages, or (in some claims) conditional fee arrangements. Regulated firms in England and Wales must publish pricing information for certain services and give you clear costs information at the outset. iComply does not publish fees; the firm will give you a POA quote.

Ask for a written estimate and for an explanation of what is not included, such as court fees, barristers' fees or experts. Ask too whether legal expenses insurance or legal aid might cover some or all of the cost.
Qualifications and registration to look for

Solicitors in England and Wales are regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA), and you can check an individual or firm on the SRA's register. Financial advisers help clients in many situations. Some of the most common are:

Once you are introduced, these questions help you decide whether the financial adviser is right for you:

  • Are you FCA authorised, and is your advice independent or restricted?
  • How do you charge for initial advice and ongoing service?
  • How will you report on performance?
  • Which platforms or providers do you typically use, and why?
  • What qualifications do you hold?
  • How do you assess my attitude to risk and capacity for loss?
When to think twice

Be cautious if you notice any of the following:

  • Not on the FCA register, or a clone firm using a real firm's name
  • Unclear or hidden charges

Advisers often charge for initial advice, then an ongoing fee for reviews, which may be fixed or a percentage of the money they look after. Firms must set out charges clearly before advising you. iComply does not publish fees; the firm quotes you, POA.

Ask for charges in pounds as well as percentages, and check what the ongoing service includes. The FCA's Consumer Duty expects firms to provide fair value.
Qualifications and registration to look for

Financial advice in the UK is regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). Check that any adviser or firm is authorised, or is an appointed representative of an authorised firm, on the FCA register. If something goes wrong you can complain to the firm, then to the Financial Ombudsman Service, and the Financial Services Compensation Scheme may protect you if an authorised firm fails.

Advisers must tell you whether their advice is independent (considering the whole market) or restricted (limited to certain products or providers), and how they charge. Chartered status from the Chartered Insurance Institute or the Personal Finance Society, and certifications such as CFP, show advanced qualifications.

Adviser and advisor are simply two spellings of the same word. What matters is whether the person giving advice is qualified and, where the law requires it, regulated for that type of advice.

iComply is not a regulator and does not provide the professional service itself. We introduce you to professionals who hold their own registrations, and we encourage you to check them on the public register.

secs: Common reasons people contact barristers

Barristers help clients in many situations. Some of the most common are:

  • A written opinion on the strength of a case before going further.
  • Mediation or negotiation support in a dispute.
  • A second opinion on advice already received.
  • Specialist advice in areas such as tax, planning or intellectual property.
  • Representation at a court or tribunal hearing.

If your situation is not listed, that is fine. Describe it in your own words and we will work out which kind of barrister fits best.
Key things to know about an intellectual property barrister

These practical points are worth knowing before you speak to anyone about an intellectual property barrister:

  • Evidence of ownership is key.
  • Act fast on infringement.

A good barrister will talk you through each of these in plain English.
Information that helps us match you

A short, clear brief saves time on both sides. Useful details include:

  • Any previous advice you have received
  • A short summary of the issue and what you want from the barrister
  • Your budget expectations, so scope can be agreed
  • Key documents, numbered and in date order
  • Whether you already have a solicitor
  • Any language or accessibility needs for hearings

Please do not send confidential records or full files in your first message. The practice will ask for what it needs securely once you are introduced.
How long things usually take

Barristers' diaries can fill weeks ahead, especially for hearings. If you have a fixed hearing date, include it prominently in your enquiry. Written advice on a straightforward point can sometimes be turned round quickly when the papers are well organised.
When to think twice

There are many osteopaths to choose from, and they are not all the same. Osteopaths use hands-on treatment, exercise and advice to help with back pain, neck pain, joint problems and muscle tension.

iComply Professional Services is a free matching service. You tell us what you need and where you are; we connect you with a suitable UK osteopath who can quote for the work. The practice provides the service, and every quote is POA.
secs: What osteopaths commonly help with

You do not need to have everything worked out. Clients often come to us with situations like these:

  • Joint stiffness that limits walking or exercise.
  • Aches during or after pregnancy.
  • Headaches that seem linked to posture or neck tension.
  • Neck and shoulder tension linked to desk work.
  • Recurring pain that has not settled with rest.

If your situation is not listed, that is fine. Describe it in your own words and we will work out which kind of osteopath fits best.
Questions to ask an osteopath

Once you are introduced, these questions help you decide whether the osteopath is right for you:

  • Do you accept my health insurance?
  • Are you registered with the statutory regulator, and can I check that online?
  • When would you suggest I see my GP instead?
  • What does treatment involve, and are there risks?
  • How many sessions do you expect I will need?
  • How will we know if it is working?
How to check you are in safe hands

"Osteopath" is a protected title in the UK. Every osteopath must be registered with the General Osteopathic Council (GOsC), which sets standards and investigates concerns. You can check the GOsC register online before you book.

Osteopaths use hands-on techniques such as massage, stretching and joint mobilisation, along with advice on exercise and posture. They assess your medical history first and should refer you to your GP if your symptoms need medical investigation.

Please note that iComply is a matching service only. We are not regulated as a osteopath, and we do not give professional advice. The practice you are introduced to is responsible for its own registration and for the work it does.
Your relationship with the practice
Once introduced, the practice will book your first appointment and agree a treatment plan with you. The practitioner is responsible for your care. iComply does not provide medical advice.
When to think twice

Be cautious if you notice any of the following:

  • Discouraging you from seeing your GP
  • Claims to treat conditions unrelated to muscles and joints
  • No statutory registration
  • Pressure to pay for many sessions in advance
What to prepare before you enquire

A short, clear brief saves time on both sides. Useful details include:

  • The days and times you can attend
  • Anything that makes it better or worse
  • How long it has been going on
  • Current medication and medical conditions
  • Any treatment you have tried already
  • Where the pain is and how it started

Please do not send confidential records or full files in your first message. The practice will ask for what it needs securely once you are introduced.

Osteopaths vary in specialism, size, fees and approach. Some focus on particular types of client; others offer a broad service. Knowing the differences helps you choose.

Looking for pension financial advisor near me usually starts with a practical problem that needs a qualified person. Pension financial advisers combine pension advice with wider planning on investments, tax and retirement income.

Rather than calling round, you can send one enquiry to iComply. We look at your needs, location and timing, then introduce you to a suitable pension advice firm. They quote you directly, POA, and you decide whether to go ahead.
secs: Common reasons people contact pension advisers

Every enquiry is different, but these are typical starting points for clients who contact pension advisers:

  • Making sure pension death benefits go to the right people.
  • Weighing up an annuity against drawdown.
  • Checking whether retirement plans are on track.
  • Pension sharing on divorce.
  • Deciding how to take money from a pension at retirement.

If your situation is not listed, that is fine. Describe it in your own words and we will work out which kind of pension adviser fits best.
Looking for a pension financial adviser close to home

When you search for a pension financial adviser near you, you usually want someone reachable, available and trustworthy. Tell us your town or postcode and we look for suitable practices nearby with capacity to help.

Near-me searches return lots of results, from directories to adverts. Our role is simpler: understand your brief and introduce a suitable professional, so you do not have to work through the list alone.
Before you choose a pension financial adviser

These practical points are worth knowing before you speak to anyone about a pension financial adviser:

  • Holistic advice spots trade-offs.
  • Death benefits matter.
  • Review regularly.

Raise any of these with the pension adviser you are introduced to; they should be happy to explain.
What happens after you are introduced

Once introduced, the firm will agree terms and gather information from your providers. Advice and responsibility sit with the authorised firm. iComply does not give financial advice. The value of pensions and investments can fall as well as rise.
How fees usually work (POA)

Pension advice is usually charged as an initial fee, sometimes with an ongoing advice fee. Specialist transfer advice is often charged separately. iComply does not publish fees; the firm quotes you, POA.

Ask whether fees can be taken from the pension, and how that affects its value.
What to prepare before you enquire

You do not need all of this to enquire, but the more you can share, the better the match:

  • Your health, which can affect annuity rates
  • Recent statements for every pension you hold
  • Beneficiary nominations
  • Your target retirement age and income
  • Any guaranteed benefits or protected tax-free cash
  • Your state pension forecast from the government's Check your State Pension service

Please do not send confidential records or full files in your first message. The practice will ask for what it needs securely once you are introduced.
How to check you are in safe hands

Financial advice in the UK is regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). Check that any adviser or firm is authorised, or is an appointed representative of an authorised firm, on the FCA register. If something goes wrong you can complain to the firm, then to the Financial Ombudsman Service, and the Financial Services Compensation Scheme may protect you if an authorised firm fails.

Some pension decisions carry special rules. Advice on transferring out of a defined benefit (final salary) scheme above a set value must come from an adviser with pension transfer specialist permissions, and safeguarded benefits deserve particular care. Free, impartial guidance is available from Pension Wise for people over 50 with defined contribution pensions.

Adviser and advisor are simply two spellings of the same word. What matters is whether the person giving advice is qualified and, where the law requires it, regulated for that type of advice.

Please note that iComply is a matching service only. We are not regulated as a pension adviser, and we do not give professional advice. The practice you are introduced to is responsible for its own registration and for the work it does.
Good questions for your first call

Once you are introduced, these questions help you decide whether the pension adviser is right for you:

  • Can you explain annuity and drawdown risks side by side?
  • How do you charge, and is it different if I do not go ahead?
  • What happens with ongoing advice and reviews?
  • How do you model income in retirement?
  • How will you check for valuable guarantees in my existing pensions?
  • What are the tax consequences of each option?
From enquiry to quote in four steps

1. Enquire for free with your town or postcode and a short description.
  2. We clarify anything unclear, so the introduction is useful from the start.
  3. We connect you with a pension financial adviser who suits your situation.
  4. The practice takes over, confirms scope and fees in writing and does the work.

There is no charge to you for the introduction, and no obligation to accept any quote.
Red flags when choosing a pension financial adviser

Most professionals are honest and competent, but it is worth knowing the warning signs:

  • Cold calls about your pension
  • Firms not on the FCA register
  • Pressure to transfer quickly
  • Overseas investments or unusual schemes
Typical timescales
Initial meetings are often available within a couple of weeks. Gathering information from pension providers can take several weeks, so start well before you need to make a decision.

A free, impartial government-backed service offering guidance to people over 50 about their options for defined contribution pensions. It is guidance, not personal advice.

If you have typed personal accountant near me into a search bar, you are likely looking for help soon and not too far away. Personal accountants help individuals with Self Assessment, capital gains, rental income, pensions and other personal tax matters.

We act as the middleman between you and the professional. Share a short brief and we match you with a personal accountant who has the right experience and capacity. Enquiring is free, and you are under no obligation to accept a quote.
secs: Common reasons people contact accountants

You do not need to have everything worked out. Clients often come to us with situations like these:

  • A business sale, restructure or investment round that needs proper numbers.
  • A VAT registration or a change of VAT scheme.
  • A growing business that needs management accounts and cash-flow forecasting.
  • A landlord with rental income from one or several properties.
  • A contractor deciding how to work and how to pay themselves.

If your situation is not listed, that is fine. Describe it in your own words and we will work out which kind of accountant fits best.
How our free matching service works

1. Tell us what you need. Use the contact form, WhatsApp or phone. A few lines is enough.
  2. We review your brief. We check the type of accountant you need, your location and your timing.
  3. We match you. We introduce a suitable practice with capacity, usually within a few working days.
  4. You get a quote. The practice quotes you directly, POA. You decide whether to go ahead.

We are the middleman, not the provider: the professional you choose carries out the work and is responsible for it.
What to ask before you instruct anyone

Once you are introduced, these questions help you decide whether the accountant is right for you:

  • Is your fee fixed for the year or based on time spent?
  • Are you a member of a professional body, and which one?
  • How do you handle Making Tax Digital requirements?
  • Who will actually prepare my accounts, and who reviews them?
  • What is included, and what would be charged as extra work?
  • Do you have experience with businesses or income like mine?
What to prepare before you enquire

You do not need all of this to enquire, but the more you can share, the better the match:

  • Your Unique Taxpayer Reference or company number
  • The type of business or income you have (sole trader, partnership, company, landlord, employee)
  • How often you want contact: once a year or monthly
  • The deadlines you know about and any letters from HMRC
  • Which software you use, if any (for example Xero, QuickBooks or Sage)
  • Whether you are VAT registered or close to the threshold

Please do not send confidential records or full files in your first message. The practice will ask for what it needs securely once you are introduced.
Your relationship with the practice

After the introduction, the practice will usually run its own onboarding: identity checks required under money-laundering rules, an engagement letter and authority to act with HMRC. From then on the relationship is between you and the accountant. You stay free to change firms later; a professional clearance letter makes handovers straightforward.
Typical timescales

Most practices can take on a new client within a few weeks, but capacity tightens sharply in the run-up to the 31 January Self Assessment deadline and around company year ends. If you have a deadline coming up, say so in your enquiry so we can prioritise practices with room to help now.
Before you choose a personal accountant

These practical points are worth knowing before you speak to anyone about a personal accountant:

  • Bring P60s, investment statements and rental figures.
  • Ask whether they can deal with HMRC on your behalf.
  • Plan for payments on account.

Raise any of these with the accountant you are introduced to; they should be happy to explain.
How to check you are in safe hands

In the UK, the word "accountant" on its own is not a protected title, so anyone can use it. Titles such as Chartered Accountant (ICAEW, ICAS or Chartered Accountants Ireland), Chartered Certified Accountant (ACCA) and Chartered Management Accountant (CIMA) are protected, and members are bound by their body's ethics, training and complaints rules. Only registered auditors can sign statutory audit reports.

Every practice offering accountancy services must also be supervised for anti-money-laundering purposes, either by a professional body or by HMRC. It is reasonable to ask which body supervises a firm, whether they hold professional indemnity insurance, and how complaints are handled.

Please note that iComply is a matching service only. We are not regulated as a accountant, and we do not give professional advice. The practice you are introduced to is responsible for its own registration and for the work it does.
What a personal accountant is likely to cost (POA)

Accountancy fees depend on the complexity of your affairs, the quality of your records and how much of the work you want the accountant to take on. Many practices offer fixed monthly or annual packages; others charge for time. Either can be fair if the scope is written down. iComply does not set or publish fees: the practice will quote you, and that quote is POA.

Ask for an engagement letter before work starts. It should list what is included, your responsibilities, deadlines and how extra work is charged. Comparing two or three written scopes is usually more useful than comparing headline prices.
Red flags when choosing a personal accountant

Most professionals are honest and competent, but it is worth knowing the warning signs:

  • No clear answer about who handles your file day to day
  • Promises of tax savings that sound too good to be true
  • No engagement letter or written scope before work begins
  • Pressure to sign up to schemes you do not understand

Yes. Your new accountant will contact the old one for professional clearance and any information they need. Tell us your timing and we will match you with a practice that can take over smoothly.

Looking for post operative physiotherapy near me usually starts with a practical problem that needs a qualified person. Post-operative physiotherapy follows your surgeon's protocol to restore movement and strength after operations such as joint replacements or ligament repairs.

Rather than calling round, you can send one enquiry to iComply. We look at your needs, location and timing, then introduce you to a suitable physiotherapy clinic. They quote you directly, POA, and you decide whether to go ahead.
secs: Common reasons people contact physiotherapists

You do not need to have everything worked out. Clients often come to us with situations like these:

  • Rehabilitation after a stroke or with a neurological condition.
  • A frozen shoulder or other painful, stiff joint.
  • An older relative who needs help with mobility at home.
  • A child with a developmental or movement problem.
  • Rehabilitation after joint replacement or other surgery.

If your situation is not listed, that is fine. Describe it in your own words and we will work out which kind of physiotherapist fits best.
Timing and urgency

Private physiotherapy appointments are often available within a few days. Recovery time depends on the problem: some settle in a few sessions, while post-operative or neurological rehabilitation can take months. Sudden severe weakness, loss of bladder or bowel control, or numbness around the groin needs urgent medical help.
What happens after you are introduced
Once introduced, the clinic will book your assessment and agree a treatment plan with you. Clinical responsibility sits with the physiotherapist. iComply does not provide medical advice.
How iComply matches you

1. Tell us what you need. Use the contact form, WhatsApp or phone. A few lines is enough.
  2. We review your brief. We check the type of physiotherapist you need, your location and your timing.
  3. We match you. We introduce a suitable practice with capacity, usually within a few working days.
  4. You get a quote. The practice quotes you directly, POA. You decide whether to go ahead.

We are the middleman, not the provider: the professional you choose carries out the work and is responsible for it.
Checking physiotherapists are qualified and regulated

"Physiotherapist" and "physical therapist" are protected titles in the UK. Anyone using them must be registered with the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC), and you can check the HCPC register online. Most physiotherapists are also members of the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy (CSP), shown by the letters MCSP.

Sports therapists, massage therapists and personal trainers can be helpful for some needs, but they are not physiotherapists. For an injury, post-surgery rehabilitation or a neurological condition, check that you are booking an HCPC-registered physiotherapist.

iComply is not a regulator and does not provide the professional service itself. We introduce you to professionals who hold their own registrations, and we encourage you to check them on the public register.

Near-me searches return lots of results, from directories to adverts. Our role is simpler: understand your brief and introduce a suitable professional, so you do not have to work through the list alone.
When to think twice

Be cautious if you notice any of the following:

  • A long block of prepaid sessions before any assessment
  • No referral back when problems do not improve
  • No HCPC registration
  • No home exercise plan or progress review
Questions to ask post-operative physiotherapy

Asking a few direct questions early tells you a lot about how a practice works:

  • Are you HCPC registered, and do you have experience with this problem?
  • Do you work with my insurer?
  • How many sessions do you usually expect for problems like this?
  • How will we measure progress?
  • Will I get exercises to do at home?
  • Do you offer home visits or video sessions?
How fees usually work (POA)

Physiotherapy is usually charged per session, with the first assessment often longer than follow-ups. Home visits, specialist neurological physiotherapy and sports rehabilitation programmes may be priced differently. iComply does not publish prices; the clinic quotes you, POA.

Ask whether your health insurer requires a GP referral or pre-authorisation, and whether the clinic bills the insurer directly.

  • Your goals, such as returning to running or walking without pain
  • Your health insurance details, if you have cover
  • Where it hurts and how the problem started

Please do not send confidential records or full files in your first message. The practice will ask for what it needs securely once you are introduced.

These practical points are worth knowing before you speak to anyone about post-operative physiotherapy:

  • Start when your surgeon advises.

What to prepare before you enquire

A short, clear brief saves time on both sides. Useful details include:

Good questions for your first call

Many surveyors are members of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS), and RICS-regulated firms must follow professional standards, hold insurance and offer a complaints process. Chartered surveyors use the letters MRICS or FRICS. Some specialist roles have their own bodies, such as the Faculty of Party Wall Surveyors or the Property Care Association for damp and timber specialists.

Check the RICS directory, ask which report type you are getting and confirm whether the surveyor is independent of the sale. For asbestos work, look for organisations accredited by UKAS for surveying.

solicitors.intro:
There are many solicitors to choose from, and they are not all the same. A solicitor gives legal advice, prepares documents, negotiates for you and, where needed, runs court cases and instructs barristers, across areas from property and family law to business and disputes.

We act as the middleman between you and the professional. Share a short brief and we match you with a solicitor who has the right experience and capacity. Enquiring is free, and you are under no obligation to accept a quote.
secs: What solicitors commonly help with

You do not need to have everything worked out. Clients often come to us with situations like these:

  • A business contract, shareholder agreement or company sale.
  • A dispute with an employer, landlord, business or neighbour.
  • A will, a lasting power of attorney or a family member's estate.
  • A debt that is owed to you, or one you are being chased for.
  • An injury or a medical treatment that went wrong.

If your situation is not listed, that is fine. Describe it in your own words and we will work out which kind of solicitor fits best.
How our free matching service works

1. Tell us what you need. Use the contact form, WhatsApp or phone. A few lines is enough.
  2. We review your brief. We check the type of solicitor you need, your location and your timing.
  3. We match you. We introduce a suitable practice with capacity, usually within a few working days.
  4. You get a quote. The practice quotes you directly, POA. You decide whether to go ahead.

There is no charge to you for the introduction, and no obligation to accept any quote.
When to think twice

Most professionals are honest and competent, but it is worth knowing the warning signs:

  • Guarantees about the outcome of a dispute
  • Pressure to sign immediately without time to read terms
  • No clear costs information or client care letter
  • Requests to send money to an account that changes by email
Key things to know about a solicitor

A few points come up again and again with a solicitor:

  • Choose a solicitor who specialises in your type of matter.
  • Ask for costs information at the start.
  • Check the firm on the SRA register.

Raise any of these with the solicitor you are introduced to; they should be happy to explain.
How solicitors differ

Solicitors vary in specialism, size, fees and approach. Some focus on particular types of client; others offer a broad service. Knowing the differences helps you choose.

Rather than searching through long lists of solicitors, tell us what you need. We introduce practices that fit, and you can compare their quotes.
How to check you are in safe hands

Solicitors in England and Wales are regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA), and you can check an individual or firm on the SRA's register. In Scotland solicitors are regulated by the Law Society of Scotland, and in Northern Ireland by the Law Society of Northern Ireland. Regulated firms must hold professional indemnity insurance and have a complaints procedure; if that does not resolve things, the Legal Ombudsman can look at service complaints in England and Wales.

The word "lawyer" is not protected on its own, so check that whoever handles your matter is a solicitor, a chartered legal executive (CILEx) or another authorised professional. Reserved activities such as conducting court litigation and certain probate and conveyancing work can only be carried out by authorised people.

Please note that iComply is a matching service only. We are not regulated as a solicitor, and we do not give professional advice. The practice you are introduced to is responsible for its own registration and for the work it does.
What to ask before you instruct anyone

Once you are introduced, these questions help you decide whether the solicitor is right for you:

  • What could make costs rise, and how will you warn me?
  • Who will handle my matter day to day, and who supervises them?
  • What are the likely next steps and timescales?
  • How much experience do you have with cases like mine?
  • What is your realistic view of my options at this stage?
  • How will you keep me updated?
Information that helps us match you

You do not need all of this to enquire, but the more you can share, the better the match:

  • The names of the other people or organisations involved
  • Copies of key documents such as contracts, letters or court papers
  • Any deadlines you have been given, especially court dates
  • A short timeline of what has happened, with dates
  • What outcome you would like
  • Whether you have legal expenses insurance (often in home or car policies)

Please do not send confidential records or full files in your first message. The practice will ask for what it needs securely once you are introduced.
What a solicitor is likely to cost (POA)

Legal fees depend on the type of matter, its complexity and who does the work. Firms commonly charge hourly rates, fixed fees for defined stages, or (in some claims) conditional fee arrangements. Regulated firms in England and Wales must publish pricing information for certain services and give you clear costs information at the outset. iComply does not publish fees; the firm will give you a POA quote.

Ask for a written estimate and for an explanation of what is not included, such as court fees, barristers' fees or experts. Ask too whether legal expenses insurance or legal aid might cover some or all of the cost.
After the introduction

After the introduction, the firm will carry out identity checks and conflict checks and send a client care letter setting out who is acting for you, what they will do and how they charge. Your legal relationship is with the firm. iComply does not give legal advice and does not take part in your case.

Tax advisers who provide services for a fee must be supervised for anti-money-laundering purposes. HMRC has also been tightening standards for paid tax agents, so it is reasonable to ask about qualifications, supervision and professional indemnity insurance before you go ahead.
